name: infrastructure
description: Roads, rails, bridges, poles and other public works.
conventions: Linear objects (roads, rails, fences) are built as a repeatable segment with matching ends, so segments tile along z.
anticipate: A segment that tiles end to end, plus curved or junction variants.
Collision and navigation surfaces separate from the visual mesh.

name: road

scale.source: lane width about 2.75-3.75 m (general knowledge: design guides differ per country); a segment is as long as you choose

pitfalls: Segments must have identical cross-sections at both ends, or seams show.
Lane markings are a decal or texture, not geometry, or they z-fight with the surface.

parts.name: Leaf
parts.note: A bascule bridge leaf hinges about a horizontal axis at its end.

scale.source: general knowledge: typical production range, not a standard

name: railway track

scale.source: ballast bed width, general knowledge; gauge is 1.435 m (UIC standard)

anticipate: Standard gauge is 1.435 m between the inner rail edges (UIC/IEC standard); sleepers about 0.6 m apart (general knowledge); the ballast bed is about 3.4-4.5 m wide.

name: street lamp
description: A lamp post or street light.

parts.name: Lamp
parts.note: Emissive material plus a light node at the bulb.

scale.source: general knowledge: typical production range, not a standard

name: fence

scale.source: general knowledge: typical production range, not a standard

anticipate: A repeatable bay with a post at each end.

parts.name: Post
parts.note: Posts at the ends and between sections; set into the ground.

name: crash barrier
description: A steel guardrail (W-beam) on posts beside a road or race track, optionally with a catch fence behind it.

parts.name: Post
parts.note: Steel posts about every 2 m (guardrail) or 4 m (catch fence).

parts.name: Rail
parts.note: The W-beam is about 0.31 m high with its centre about 0.55-0.75 m above the ground; motorsport uses two or three stacked.

scale.source: general knowledge: road and motorsport guardrail sections; not a standard

anticipate: A repeatable section with a post at each end; tile sections along the edge of the run-off area, not along the track edge.

name: race kerb
description: A low red-and-white kerb at the edge of a race track in a corner.

parts.name: Block
parts.note: Alternating red and white blocks about 1-1.5 m long; the kerb rises a few centimetres towards the outside.

scale.source: general knowledge: circuit kerbs; not a standard

anticipate: Kerbs run on the inside of a corner along the apex and on the outside at the exit; they lie on the track surface, not on the grass.

name: power pylon
description: A high-voltage pylon or utility pole.

scale.source: general knowledge: typical production range, not a standard: wooden poles 8-15 m, lattice pylons 25-70 m

parts.name: Leg
parts.note: The lattice legs lean in towards the top.

name: canal lock
description: A navigation lock: a chamber between two gated heads that lifts or lowers boats between two water levels.

parts.name: Chamber
parts.note: Concrete or brick walls with the water inside; the water level inside moves between the two outside levels.

parts.name: Gate
parts.note: Mitre gates come in pairs per head and close in a V that points upstream (towards the higher water); lift gates rise in a tall frame instead.

parts.name: Fender
parts.note: Guide walls and dolphins in front of each head, where boats wait.

parts.name: Signal
parts.note: Red/green lights at each head: red = wait, green = enter.

scale.source: general knowledge of European inland locks: small polder locks about 30-50 x 5-7.5 m, CEMT class Va canal locks about 200-280 x 12.5-16 m, large sea locks up to about 500 x 70 m; lift 0.3-3 m inland, up to about 5 m with tides

conventions: The chamber's long axis is the direction of travel; build the gates as separate nodes with their pivot on the hinge so they can be animated.
Each side of the lock has its own water level; the chamber surface is a separate mesh so its height can move.
anticipate: Gates that open when a boat approaches and close behind it, with the signal lights following the state.
A waiting area with dolphins on both sides, and a road or footpath over one head.
pitfalls: A lock with the same water level on both sides is decoration: give the two reaches their own levels, or the chamber has nothing to do.
Boats that steer by an offset from the centreline must aim for the centre inside the chamber, or they clip the walls.
Mitre gates drawn pointing downstream would be pushed open by the water.

name: harbour basin
description: An inland harbour: a dug basin off a canal or river, with quay walls, bollards, cranes and sheds.

parts.name: Basin
parts.note: Deeper than the boats' draught; joined to the waterway by its open end.

parts.name: Quay
parts.note: A flat apron about 1.5 m above the water with a vertical wall to the water and a fender beam.

parts.name: AccessRoad
parts.note: Connected to the road graph, or traffic and emergency routes never reach it.

scale.source: general knowledge: marinas and small village harbours 40-200 m, inland cargo basins 150-1000 m long and 50-150 m wide, port basins larger; quay about 1.5-2 m above the water

conventions: Place the basin so its open end joins the waterway's water surface; the quay height is one value shared by the walls, bollards and sheds.
anticipate: Moored boats along the quay, lights on masts, and a road that joins the road network.
pitfalls: A basin dug only in the visual mesh but not in the terrain heights (or in only one of several terrain grids) shows land through the water.
Buildings left standing where the basin was dug: remove them and rebuild any spatial index that pointed at them.
